claims.claim: Increased ROS in CPT1 knockdown endothelial cells has been reported in another study.
claims.source: A similar observation of increased ROS in CPT1 knockdown endothelial cells has been reported in another study (Kalucka et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference showing similar ROS increase in CPT1 knockdown in another cell type.

claims.claim: L-carnitine is often used as a supplement for enhancing fat oxidation.
claims.source: Due to the central role of carnitine in fat metabolism, it is often used as a supplement for enhancing fat oxidation (Pekala et al., 2011; Wall et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references supporting the use of L-carnitine to enhance FAO.

claims.claim: FAO can be upregulated in cells by L-carnitine supplementation.
claims.source: Several studies have concluded that FAO can be upregulated in the cells by L-carnitine supplementation (Pekala et al., 2011; Sahlin, 2011; Wall et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The results section cites multiple references supporting L-carnitine's effect on FAO.

claims.claim: The lymph gland from L-carnitine fed larvae exhibits a drastic reduction in progenitor zone with a concomitant increase in differentiation.
claims.source: Compared to control (Figure 4A), the lymph gland from L-carnitine fed larvae (96 hr AEH) exhibits a drastic reduction in progenitor zone (visualized by dome > GFP) with a concomitant increase in differentiation (visualized by P1: Nimrod; Figure 4B–C).
claims.evidence: The results section describes L-carnitine supplementation experiments shown in Figure 4A-C.

claims.claim: Feeding L-carnitine could rescue the differentiation defects associated with whd1 heterozygous mutants.
claims.source: The increase in differentiation by L-carnitine supplementation is also apparent in whd1 heterozygous mutants. Feeding L-carnitine could rescue the differentitaion defects associated with whd1 heterozygous mutants (Compare Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
claims.evidence: The results section describes rescue experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E.

claims.claim: Overexpression of whd results in an increase in the differentiation of hemocyte progenitors.
claims.source: Overexpression of whd indeed results in an increase in the differentiation of hemocyte progenitors (compare Figure 4D with Figure 4E–F).
claims.evidence: The results section describes whd overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4D-F.

claims.claim: The otherwise undifferentiated reserve progenitors of the secondary lobes differentiate upon whd overexpression.
claims.source: It is interesting to note that the otherwise undifferentiated reserve progenitors of the secondary lobes also differentiate upon whd overexpression (marked by a dotted white line in Figure 4G–H).
claims.evidence: The results section describes observations from Figure 4G-H showing differentiation in secondary lobes.

claims.claim: Early third instar lymph glands from L-carnitine fed larvae exhibit a radical decline in EdU incorporation compared to control.
claims.source: The early third instar lymph glands from L-carnitine fed larvae exhibit a radical decline in EdU incorporation compared to the proliferating progenitors of the control larvae of similar age (compare Figure 4I–I' with Figure 4J-J' and quantified in Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: The results section describes EdU incorporation assay results shown in Figure 4I-K.

claims.claim: Overexpression of whd in progenitors led to a decline in EdU incorporation.
claims.source: As a genetic correlate, we overexpressed whd in the progenitors, which also led to a decline in EdU incorporation (Figure 4L–N).
claims.evidence: The results section describes EdU incorporation assay results shown in Figure 4L-N.

claims.claim: FUCCI analysis reveals an abundance of G2-M progenitors in early third instar larvae reared in L-carnitine supplemented food compared to control.
claims.source: Our FUCCI analysis reveals an abundance of G2-M progenitors in the early third instar larvae reared in L-carnitine supplemented food compared to control samples.
claims.evidence: The results section describes FUCCI analysis results.

claims.claim: Upon FAO upregulation, the progenitor experiences a precocious G2-M halt in their cell cycle.
claims.source: Thus, less EdU incorporation due to upregulated FAO resulted in an early onset of G2-M arrest in the progenitors (compare Figure 4O–O' with Figure 4P–P' and quantified in Figure 4Q).
claims.evidence: The results section describes FUCCI analysis results shown in Figure 4O-Q.

claims.claim: ATP levels of homozygous whd1 larvae are comparable to similarly aged control.
claims.source: Quite intriguingly, ATP levels of homozygous whd1 larvae are comparable to similarly aged control (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The results section describes ATP measurement results shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Higher proliferation is driven by elevated glycolysis in different scenarios.
claims.source: Since higher proliferation is driven by elevated glycolysis in different scenarios (Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011), we hypothesized that loss of FAO might push the progenitors towards a higher glycolytic index.
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference supporting the relationship between proliferation and glycolysis.

claims.claim: In control, late third instar Dome+ progenitors exhibit low glucose uptake compared to peripheral hemocyte population marked by Hml.
claims.source: In control, late third instar Dome+ progenitors exhibit low glucose uptake (Figure 5B–B'' and Figure 5D) compared to the higher uptake detectable in the peripheral hemocyte population marked by Hml (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–A''' and quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The results section describes glucose uptake assay results shown in Figure 5B-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Higher glucose uptake is evident in the FAO mutant progenitors.
claims.source: In sharp contrast, higher glucose uptake is evident in the FAO mutant progenitors (Figure 5C–C'' and quantified in Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The results section describes glucose uptake assay results shown in Figure 5C-D.

claims.claim: In vivo lactate dehydrogenase assay revealed a high glycolytic index prevalent in the lymph glands of homozygous whd1.
claims.source: In concordance with the above result, in vivo lactate dehydrogenase assay (Abu-Shumays and Fristrom, 1997) also revealed a high glycolytic index prevalent in the lymph glands of homozygous whd1 (Figure 5E–F).
claims.evidence: The results section describes lactate dehydrogenase assay results shown in Figure 5E-F with citation for the method.

claims.claim: In the whd1 lymph gland, the transcript levels of HexA and Pfk exhibit a 1.6 fold and 1.7 fold increase in their expression, respectively.
claims.source: Moreover, in the whd1 lymph gland, the transcript levels of HexA (Hexokinase A) and Pfk (Phosphofructokinase), the enzymes involved in the two irreversible steps of glycolysis: exhibit a 1.6 fold and 1.7 fold increase in their expression, respectively (Figure 5G–H).
claims.evidence: The results section describes qRT-PCR results shown in Figure 5G-H.

claims.claim: Upon rearing whd1 homozygous larvae in food supplemented with 2-DG, the hyper-proliferating hemocyte progenitors demonstrate a significant drop in EdU incorporation to a level comparable to control.
claims.source: Upon rearing whd1 homozygous larvae in food supplemented with glycolysis inhibitor 2-Deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), the otherwise hyper-proliferating hemocyte progenitors (EdU, Figure 5J) demonstrate a significant drop in EdU incorporation to a level that is comparable to control (compare Figure 5K with Figure 5I, and quantified in Figure 5M).
claims.evidence: The results section describes 2-DG treatment experiments shown in Figure 5I-M.

claims.claim: The glycolytic block by feeding 2-DG does not restore the abrogated differentiation observed in homozygous whd1 hemocyte progenitors.
claims.source: Although the glycolytic block by feeding 2-DG rescues the cell cycle status, the abrogated differentiation observed in homozygous whd1 hemocyte progenitors is not restored (compare Figure 5P with Figure 5O and N and quantified in Figure 5R).
claims.evidence: The results section describes 2-DG treatment experiments shown in Figure 5N-R.

claims.claim: Inhibition of glucose uptake by genetic perturbation of Glut1 in progenitor specific manner in the FAO mutant does not restore differentiation.
claims.source: Inhibition of glucose uptake by genetic perturbation of glucose transporter Glut1 in progenitor specific manner in the FAO mutant also endorses the above result (Figure 5L–L' and M, and Figure 5Q–R).
claims.evidence: The results section describes Glut1 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5L-M and Q-R.

claims.claim: Histone acetylation mediated by Histone Acetyl Transferases (HATs) directly controls the expression of differentiation factor, thereby regulating germline stem cell differentiation.
claims.source: Histone acetylation mediated by Histone Acetyl Transferases (HATs) directly controls the expression of differentiation factor, thereby regulating germline stem cell differentiation (McCarthy et al., 2018; Xin et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references supporting HATs' role in stem cell differentiation.

claims.claim: Loss of Histone Acetyl Transferase (HAT) genes, Gcn5 and chm, phenocopy the differentiation defect seen in the hemocyte progenitors of FAO loss of function.
claims.source: Quite strikingly, loss of Histone Acetyl Transferase (HAT) genes, Gcn5 (Carré et al., 2005) and chm (chameau) (Grienenberger et al., 2002; Miotto et al., 2006) phenocopy the differentiation defect seen in the hemocyte progenitors of FAO loss of function (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: The results section describes HAT knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6A-C with citations for the genes.

claims.claim: Downregulation of Acetyl Coenzyme A synthase/AcCoAS results in a phenotype identical to HAT or FAO loss.
claims.source: Additionally, downregulation of Acetyl Coenzyme A synthase/AcCoAS (the Drosophila orthologue of ACSS2) (Mews et al., 2017) results in a phenotype identical to HAT or FAO loss (Figure 6D) confirming the essential role of acetylation in hemocyte progenitor differentiation.
claims.evidence: The results section describes AcCoAS knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6D with citation for the gene.

claims.claim: Trans-heterozygous loss-of-function allelic combinations of whd1 with either ATPCL01466 or seaEP3364 phenocopy differentiation defects seen in whd1 homozygous lymph gland.
claims.source: Trans-heterozygous loss-of-function allelic combinations of whd1 with either ATPCL01466 (Figure 6F) or seaEP3364 (Figure 6G) phenocopy differentiation defects seen in whd1 homozygous lymph gland (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The results section describes genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 6E-G.

claims.claim: Knockdown of CPT1 leads to a reduced level of H3K9 acetylation in lymphatic endothelial cells.
claims.source: Knockdown of the rate-limiting enzyme of FAO:CPT1, leads to a reduced level of H3K9 acetylation in lymphatic endothelial cells (Wong et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference showing H3K9 acetylation defects upon CPT1 knockdown in another cell type.

claims.claim: whd1 homozygous larvae have low levels of H3K9 acetylation compared to control.
claims.source: Immunoblot analysis of extracted histones with antibody against acetylated anti-H3K9 reveals that whd1 homozygous larvae have low levels of H3K9 acetylation (Figure 6I–J) when compared to control.
claims.evidence: The results section describes Western blot results shown in Figure 6I-J.

claims.claim: The clonal patches positively marked with GFP (where whd has been downregulated) show a significant drop in H3K9 acetylation levels compared to surrounding hemocyte progenitors.
claims.source: The clonal patches positively marked with GFP (where whd has been downregulated) show a significant drop in H3K9 acetylation levels (Figure 6M–N) compared to surrounding hemocyte progenitors.
claims.evidence: The results section describes clonal analysis results shown in Figure 6M-N.

claims.claim: Histone H4 acetylation visualized by pan anti-H4 acetylation antibody reveals a drastic drop in whd knockdown clonal patches.
claims.source: Likewise, histone H4 acetylation visualized by pan anti-H4 acetylation antibody reveals a drastic drop in whd knockdown clonal patches (Figure 6O–P).
claims.evidence: The results section describes clonal analysis results shown in Figure 6O-P.

claims.claim: Upon progenitor specific downregulation of whd function, a decline in the level of both H3K9 acetylation and pan H4 acetylation is evident.
claims.source: Further, upon progenitor specific downregulation of whd function, a decline in the level of both H3K9 acetylation (compare Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–H' with Figure 6—figure supplement 1I–I' and J) and pan H4 acetylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1K–K' with Figure 6—figure supplement 1L–L' and M) is evident.
claims.evidence: The results section describes immunostaining results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H-M.

claims.claim: Compromised histone acetylation levels can be restored by supplementing acetate.
claims.source: It has been established earlier that compromised histone acetylation levels can be restored by supplementing acetate (Carrisi et al., 2008; Wellen et al., 2009; Wong et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references supporting acetate supplementation as a method to restore histone acetylation.

claims.claim: Acetate feeding does not affect progenitor differentiation in control.
claims.source: Intriguingly, acetate feeding does not affect progenitor differentiation in control, whereas it rescues the differentiation defects seen in homozygous whd1 hemocyte progenitors (Figure 7A–E).
claims.evidence: The results section describes acetate supplementation experiments shown in Figure 7A-E.

claims.claim: Acetate feeding rescues the differentiation defects seen in homozygous whd1 hemocyte progenitors.
claims.source: Intriguingly, acetate feeding does not affect progenitor differentiation in control, whereas it rescues the differentiation defects seen in homozygous whd1 hemocyte progenitors (Figure 7A–E).
claims.evidence: The results section describes acetate supplementation experiments shown in Figure 7A-E.

claims.claim: Acetate supplementation to whd1 mutant larvae leads to a restoration of the H3K9 acetylation level.
claims.source: At the molecular level, we observed that acetate supplementation to whd1 mutant larvae leads to a restoration of the H3K9 acetylation level (Figure 7F–G), which might lead to the rescue of the differentiation defect (Figure 7A–E).
claims.evidence: The results section describes Western blot results shown in Figure 7F-G.

claims.claim: Acetate supplementation restores the compromised acetylation status in the whd1 lymph gland.
claims.source: Figure 7H–L reveals that acetate supplementation indeed restores the compromised acetylation status in the whd1 lymph gland (compare Figure 7J–J' with Figure 7K–K').
claims.evidence: The results section describes immunostaining results shown in Figure 7H-L.

claims.claim: Upregulation of FAO by L-carnitine feeding leads to elevated H3K9 acetylation in the lymph gland.
claims.source: Conversely, upregulation of FAO by L-carnitine feeding leads to elevated H3K9 acetylation in the lymph gland (compare Figure 7M–M' with Figure 7N–N' and quantified in Figure 7O).
claims.evidence: The results section describes immunostaining results shown in Figure 7M-O.

claims.claim: The level of H3K9 acetylation in L-carnitine fed larvae demonstrates a significant upregulation when compared to age-isogenised non-fed control larvae.
claims.source: Likewise, the level of H3K9 acetylation in L-carnitine fed larvae demonstrates a significant upregulation when compared to age-isogenised non-fed control larvae (Figure 7P–Q).
claims.evidence: The results section describes Western blot results shown in Figure 7P-Q.

claims.claim: Jun-Kinase and dFOXO mediated signal has been previously implicated for hemocyte progenitor differentiation.
claims.source: Jun-Kinase and dFOXO (Forkhead box O) mediated signal has been previously implicated for hemocyte progenitor differentiation (Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference supporting JNK and FOXO's role in progenitor differentiation.

claims.claim: Expression of a dominant-negative allele of basket (bsk, Drosophila orthologue of Jun-Kinase) in the progenitors results in stalled differentiation.
claims.source: Analogous to whd1 lymph glands, expression of a dominant-negative allele of basket (bsk, Drosophila orthologue of Jun-Kinase) in the progenitors results in stalled differentiation (Figure 8A–C).
claims.evidence: The results section describes bsk dominant-negative experiments shown in Figure 8A-C.

claims.claim: Overexpression of FOXO pushes the progenitor fate towards precocious differentiation.
claims.source: On the other hand, overexpression of FOXO, pushes the progenitor fate towards precocious differentiation (Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009; Figure 8D–E and Figure 8H).
claims.evidence: The results section describes FOXO overexpression experiments shown in Figure 8D-E and H with citation.

claims.claim: Genetic removal of one copy of whd is sufficient to prevent the precocious differentiation observed in progenitor-specific overexpression of FOXO.
claims.source: However, genetic removal of one copy of whd is sufficient enough to prevent the precocious differentiation as observed in progenitor-specific overexpression of FOXO (Figure 8F–H).
claims.evidence: The results section describes genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 8F-H.

claims.claim: The transcript level of CPT1/whd indicates a ~41% drop upon down-regulation of bsk from hemocyte progenitors.
claims.source: The transcript level of CPT1/whd indicates a ~ 41% drop (Figure 8I) while the expression of rest of the enzymes either exhibited a mild drop (~18% in yip2) or no significant alteration upon loss of bsk from the progenitors.
claims.evidence: The results section describes qRT-PCR results shown in Figure 8I.

claims.claim: JNK controls the transcription of CPT1/whd, thereby regulating FAO.
claims.source: This observation established that JNK controls the transcription of CPT1/whd, thereby regulating FAO.
claims.evidence: The results section draws this conclusion from the qRT-PCR data showing whd transcript reduction upon bsk knockdown.

claims.claim: Clonal analyses of bsk/JNK knockdown in hemocyte progenitors reveals a drop in the levels of H3K9 acetylation and H4 pan acetylation.
claims.source: Interestingly, clonal analyses of bsk/JNK knockdown in hemocyte progenitors reveals a drop in the levels of H3K9 acetylation (Figure 8L–M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–A''') and H4 pan acetylation (Figure 8N–O and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–B''') similar to whd downregulated clonal patches (Figure 6M–P).
claims.evidence: The results section describes clonal analysis results shown in Figure 8L-O and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Hemocyte progenitors that lacked JNK when reared in acetate supplemented food demonstrate differentiation levels comparable to control.
claims.source: Indeed, the hemocyte progenitors that lacked JNK (dome >bskDN) when reared in acetate supplemented food, demonstrate differentiation levels comparable to the similarly-aged control (Figure 8P–T).
claims.evidence: The results section describes acetate supplementation rescue experiments shown in Figure 8P-T.

claims.claim: Upregulation of FAO in hemocyte progenitors that lacked JNK by L-carnitine supplementation or by overexpression of whd facilitates differentiation.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that the upregulation of FAO in hemocyte progenitors that lacked JNK indeed elicits differentiation (Figure 8U–Y and Figure 8—figure supplement 1L–P).
claims.evidence: The results section describes rescue experiments shown in Figure 8U-Y and Figure 8—figure supplement 1L-P.

claims.claim: JNK regulates the differentiation of hemocyte progenitors by FAO-mediated histone acetylation.
claims.source: Collectively, these results are in agreement with the fact that JNK regulates the differentiation of hemocyte progenitors by FAO-mediated histone acetylation.
claims.evidence: The results section draws this conclusion from the collective experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Activated JNK leads to transcriptional induction of whd to facilitate the import of fat moiety into mitochondria for β-oxidation.
claims.source: We show that activated JNK, in turn, leads to transcriptional induction of whd to facilitate the import of fat moiety into mitochondria for β-oxidation.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the findings showing JNK's regulation of whd transcription.

claims.claim: Optimal level of acetyl-CoA, the end product of FAO, is critical for the acetylation of several proteins, including histones.
claims.source: Optimal level of acetyl-CoA, the end product of FAO, is critical for the acetylation of several proteins, including histones.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the findings about acetyl-CoA's role in acetylation.

claims.claim: Altering the ROS-JNK-FAO pathway either at the level of JNK or FAO affects histone acetylation in a HAT dependent manner.
claims.source: Altering this pathway either at the level of JNK or FAO affects histone acetylation in a HAT dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the findings about the pathway's effect on histone acetylation.

claims.claim: Precocious differentiation of blood progenitors in the lymph gland of starved larvae might be an outcome of starvation induced fat mobilization and increased FAO.
claims.source: On the other hand, it is quite possible that precocious differentiation of blood progenitors in the lymph gland of starved larvae (Shim et al., 2012) might be an outcome of starvation induced fat mobilization and increased FAO.
claims.evidence: The discussion speculates about the mechanism of starvation-induced differentiation with citation.

claims.claim: JNK signaling has been associated with histone acetylation in different biological processes.
claims.source: JNK signaling has been associated with histone acetylation in different biological processes (Miotto et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites references supporting JNK's association with histone acetylation.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, Fos, a transcriptional activator of JNK, interacts with Chm (HAT) and causes modification of histones.
claims.source: In Drosophila, Fos, a transcriptional activator of JNK, interacts with Chm (HAT) and causes modification of histones.
claims.evidence: The discussion describes a known mechanism of JNK-mediated histone modification.

claims.claim: Upon downregulation of JNK and Chm, differentiation of hemocyte progenitors is halted.
claims.source: Our investigation reveals that indeed upon downregulation of JNK (Figure 8A–C) and Chm (Figure 6A–B), differentiation of hemocyte progenitors is halted.
claims.evidence: The discussion references experimental results from Figures 8A-C and 6A-B.

claims.claim: Halt in differentiation upon JNK loss is associated with alteration of the acetylation profile of H3K9 and H4.
claims.source: Further, we show that halt in differentiation upon JNK loss is associated with alteration of the acetylation profile of H3K9 and H4.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes findings about histone acetylation changes upon JNK loss.

claims.claim: Despite having high ROS levels, hemocytes fail to differentiate if FAO is attenuated.
claims.source: As a result, despite having high ROS levels, the hemocytes fail to differentiate if FAO is attenuated.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes findings about the relationship between ROS, FAO, and differentiation.

claims.claim: Upon disruption of FAO, hematopoietic progenitors adopt glycolysis to overcome the G2-M arrest but fail to initiate differentiation.
claims.source: Our results show that upon disruption of FAO, hematopoietic progenitors adopt glycolysis to overcome the G2-M arrest but fail to initiate differentiation.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes findings about metabolic adaptation in FAO mutants.

claims.claim: Pharmacological and genetic inhibition of glycolysis in the FAO mutant restores their cell cycle defect but fails to facilitate their differentiation.
claims.source: Pharmacological and genetic inhibition of glycolysis in the FAO mutant restores their cell cycle defect but fails to facilitate their differentiation.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes findings about glycolysis inhibition experiments.

claims.claim: The glycolytic surge in FAO mutants is not capable to take them through the differentiation process.
claims.source: The glycolytic surge in FAO mutants is not capable to take them through the differentiation process.
claims.evidence: The discussion draws this conclusion from the glycolysis inhibition experiments.

claims.claim: For the process of differentiation, the acetyl moiety derived from FAO plays a key role to facilitate hemocyte progenitor differentiation.
claims.source: This indicates that for the process of differentiation, the acetyl moiety derived from FAO plays a key role to facilitate hemocyte progenitor differentiation.
claims.evidence: The discussion draws this conclusion from the collective experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Alteration in acetyl-CoA levels can affect proteome and cellular metabolism by modulating intracellular crosstalk.
claims.source: A recent study has demonstrated that alteration in acetyl-CoA levels can affect proteome and cellular metabolism by modulating intracellular crosstalk (Dieterich et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The supplemented acetate is converted into the end product of FAO: acetyl-CoA, the metabolite that is essential for histone acetylation.

claims.claim: Genetically downregulating AcCoAs from the progenitor leads to a halt in their differentiation.

claims.claim: For hemocyte progenitor differentiation, the metabolic process FAO involves its metabolite acetyl-CoA for epigenetic modification.

claims.claim: Compromised in vivo histone acetylation defects can be rescued by acetate supplementation in diverse model systems.

claims.claim: FAO has been implicated in HSCs maintenance downstream of the PML-Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPARδ) pathway.

claims.claim: Upon short term starvation, there is a decline in the number of HSC in mice.

claims.claim: Several molecular mechanisms that regulate Drosophila lymph gland hematopoiesis are essential players in progenitor-based hematopoiesis in vertebrates.
claims.source: Interestingly, several molecular mechanisms that regulate Drosophila lymph gland hematopoiesis are essential players in progenitor-based hematopoiesis in vertebrates (Banerjee et al., 2019; Gold and Brückner, 2014; Krzemien et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites references supporting conservation of hematopoietic mechanisms between Drosophila and vertebrates.

results.result: Loss of FAO through genetic or pharmacological means prevents hemocyte progenitor differentiation in the Drosophila lymph gland. Multiple independent approaches (whd1 null allele, RNAi knockdown, CRISPR/Cas9 knockout, Hnf4 knockdown, Mtpα/β knockouts, and FAO inhibitors Etomoxir and Mildronate) all demonstrate that FAO-deficient progenitors accumulate without differentiating into mature hemocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C33-C42 provide convergent evidence from multiple genetic and pharmacological approaches showing that FAO loss blocks progenitor differentiation. The use of independent alleles, RNAi lines, CRISPR/Cas9, and chemical inhibitors provides strong support. Temporal analysis (C34-C36) shows early onset of the defect. The consistency across approaches and the quantitative data strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Loss of FAO causes hemocyte progenitors to become hyperproliferative rather than undergoing G2-M arrest. whd1 mutant progenitors show increased EdU incorporation and more cells in S-phase compared to control, along with elevated Ci155 expression indicating high maintenance signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 and C48 demonstrate that FAO loss disrupts the normal G2-M arrest that precedes differentiation. The EdU incorporation data (C43) and FUCCI analysis (C45-C46) provide complementary evidence. The elevated Ci155 (C48) correlates with the proliferative phenotype. The quantitative analysis showing >3-fold increase in S-phase cells is compelling.

results.result: Despite elevated ROS levels in whd1 mutant progenitors, differentiation is blocked, indicating that FAO acts downstream of ROS in the differentiation pathway. This contradicts the expectation that low ROS would explain the differentiation defect.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 establish that ROS levels are actually elevated (not reduced) in FAO mutants, which is counterintuitive given the differentiation block. The DHE staining data (C51) and supporting citation from endothelial cells (C52) provide evidence. This is a key finding showing FAO acts downstream of ROS-JNK signaling.

results.result: Upregulation of FAO by L-carnitine supplementation or whd overexpression promotes precocious differentiation of hemocyte progenitors. L-carnitine feeding reduces the progenitor zone and increases differentiation, rescues whd1 heterozygous defects, and even induces differentiation in normally quiescent secondary lobe progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 demonstrate sufficiency of FAO for differentiation through gain-of-function approaches. The L-carnitine supplementation (C55-C56) and genetic overexpression (C57-C58) provide complementary evidence. The rescue of heterozygous mutants (C56) and differentiation of secondary lobes (C58) are particularly compelling. The citations supporting L-carnitine's mechanism (C53-C54) strengthen the interpretation.

results.result: FAO upregulation causes precocious G2-M arrest in progenitors. L-carnitine feeding and whd overexpression both reduce EdU incorporation and increase the proportion of G2-M arrested cells in early third instar larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 show that FAO upregulation accelerates the cell cycle transition to G2-M arrest. The EdU data (C59-C60) and FUCCI analysis (C61-C62) are complementary. This connects FAO to the normal developmental program where G2-M arrest precedes differentiation. The consistency between pharmacological and genetic approaches strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Loss of FAO causes a metabolic shift to glycolysis in hemocyte progenitors. Despite normal ATP levels, whd1 mutants show increased glucose uptake, elevated lactate dehydrogenase activity, and increased expression of glycolytic enzymes HexA and Pfk.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 demonstrate a compensatory metabolic shift to glycolysis upon FAO loss. The normal ATP levels (C63) indicate energy production is maintained. The 2-NBDG uptake assay (C65-C66), lactate dehydrogenase assay (C67), and qRT-PCR data (C68) provide convergent evidence. The citation supporting the proliferation-glycolysis link (C64) contextualizes the findings.

results.result: Glycolysis inhibition rescues the hyperproliferation but not the differentiation defect in FAO mutants. Treatment with 2-DG or Glut1 knockdown restores normal EdU incorporation but fails to restore differentiation in whd1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 demonstrate that glycolysis is responsible for hyperproliferation but not the differentiation block. The 2-DG experiments (C69-C70) and Glut1 knockdown (C71) provide independent evidence. This dissociation between proliferation and differentiation is a key finding showing that the acetyl moiety from FAO, not just ATP production, is critical for differentiation.

results.result: Histone acetylation is required for hemocyte progenitor differentiation. Loss of HATs (Gcn5, chm) or AcCoAS phenocopies FAO loss, and genetic interactions between whd1 and acetyl-CoA pathway genes (ATPCL, sea) support a role for acetylation in differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 establish that histone acetylation machinery is required for differentiation. The HAT knockdowns (C73) and AcCoAS knockdown (C74) phenocopy FAO loss. The genetic interactions (C75) support the pathway connection. The citation for HATs in germline stem cells (C72) provides precedent. The convergence of evidence is strong.

results.result: Loss of FAO reduces histone H3K9 and H4 acetylation in hemocyte progenitors. Western blot analysis of whd1 larvae and immunostaining of whd knockdown clones both show decreased acetylation levels compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 demonstrate that FAO loss causes histone hypoacetylation. The Western blot data (C77) and clonal analysis (C78-C80) provide complementary evidence at whole-organism and tissue levels. The citation from endothelial cells (C76) provides precedent. The specificity for acetylation marks (not total H3) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Acetate supplementation rescues both histone acetylation and differentiation defects in FAO mutants. Acetate feeding restores H3K9 acetylation levels and rescues differentiation in whd1 mutants without affecting control larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 demonstrate that acetate bypasses the FAO requirement by directly providing acetyl-CoA. The rescue of both molecular (C84-C85) and cellular (C82-C83) phenotypes is compelling. The specificity (no effect on control, C82) strengthens the interpretation. The citations supporting acetate supplementation (C81) provide precedent across model systems.

results.result: FAO upregulation increases histone H3K9 acetylation. L-carnitine feeding elevates H3K9 acetylation levels in both immunostaining and Western blot analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 show that FAO upregulation increases histone acetylation, complementing the loss-of-function data. The immunostaining (C86) and Western blot (C87) provide convergent evidence. This bidirectional relationship between FAO and histone acetylation strengthens the mechanistic model.

results.result: JNK signaling regulates progenitor differentiation and genetically interacts with FAO. Expression of dominant-negative bsk blocks differentiation similar to whd1, while FOXO overexpression-induced precocious differentiation is suppressed by removing one copy of whd.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 establish genetic interactions between JNK signaling and FAO. The bsk dominant-negative phenotype (C89) phenocopies whd1. The suppression of FOXO overexpression by whd heterozygosity (C91) demonstrates epistasis. The citation for JNK/FOXO in differentiation (C88) provides context. The bidirectional genetic interactions are compelling.

results.result: JNK transcriptionally regulates whd/CPT1 expression. qRT-PCR analysis shows ~41% reduction in whd transcript levels upon bsk knockdown, while other FAO enzyme transcripts are largely unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 demonstrate transcriptional regulation of whd by JNK. The qRT-PCR data showing specific reduction of whd (C92) without major effects on other FAO enzymes supports direct regulation. However, the claim of transcriptional control (C93) is an inference from transcript levels; chromatin immunoprecipitation or promoter analysis would provide stronger evidence. The specificity for whd is notable.

results.result: JNK loss reduces histone H3K9 and H4 acetylation in hemocyte progenitors. Clonal analysis of bsk knockdown shows decreased acetylation similar to whd knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 demonstrates that JNK regulates histone acetylation, likely through its control of whd expression. The clonal analysis provides cell-autonomous evidence. The similarity to whd knockdown phenotype supports the pathway model. This connects signaling to epigenetic regulation.

results.result: Acetate supplementation or FAO upregulation rescues differentiation defects caused by JNK loss. Acetate feeding, L-carnitine supplementation, or whd overexpression all restore differentiation in bsk dominant-negative progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 demonstrate that FAO acts downstream of JNK by showing that bypassing FAO (acetate) or upregulating it (L-carnitine, whd overexpression) rescues JNK loss. The multiple rescue approaches provide strong epistatic evidence. This establishes the ROS-JNK-FAO-acetylation pathway for differentiation.

results.result: Late third instar hemocyte progenitors express high levels of Hnf4 and contain abundant neutral lipids compared to pre-progenitors and intermediate progenitors. FAO pathway genes including whd (Drosophila CPT1) are expressed in the late lymph gland.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 establish that progenitors have the molecular machinery and substrates for FAO. The Hnf4 expression (C24), lipid accumulation (C25), and FAO gene expression (C27) provide convergent evidence. The identification of whd as CPT1 (C26) is based on established homology. These descriptive findings set up the functional studies.

results.result: Hemocyte progenitors contain abundant reticular mitochondria compared to differentiated hemocytes. This mitochondrial morphology is consistent with active FAO in progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 provide morphological evidence for mitochondrial differences between progenitors and differentiated cells. The citation for FAO biochemistry (C28) and the imaging data (C29-C30) support the interpretation. However, mitochondrial morphology alone is not definitive evidence for FAO activity. This is supportive but not conclusive evidence.

results.result: The whd1 allele is a null mutation of the Drosophila CPT1 ortholog that blocks mitochondrial FAO.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 establish the genetic tool used in the study. Both claims cite published characterizations of the whd1 allele. This is essential methodological information but not a novel finding of this study.

results.result: The Drosophila lymph gland consists of a primary lobe with distinct zones: a medullary zone containing progenitors, a cortical zone with differentiated cells, and intermediate progenitors between them. Late larval progenitors are G2-M arrested, have high ROS, lack differentiation markers, are multipotent, and are maintained by the PSC niche.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C23 provide background on the lymph gland system. These are well-established facts from prior literature (multiple citations provided). This contextual information is necessary for understanding the experimental system but represents prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Metabolism regulates stem cell fate through both bioenergetic and epigenetic mechanisms. FAO is active in stem and progenitor cells and produces acetyl-CoA that can be used for energy production or protein acetylation. However, the metabolic requirements of progenitors are not fully understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C14 provide literature context for the study. All claims are supported by multiple citations to prior work. Claim C9 identifies the knowledge gap that motivates the study. This is standard background information establishing the rationale for the research.

results.result: The study establishes a signaling cascade where ROS activates JNK, which transcriptionally induces whd to promote FAO. The resulting acetyl-CoA is critical for histone acetylation in a HAT-dependent manner, and this pathway is essential for progenitor differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 summarize the main mechanistic model from the discussion. These are synthesis statements drawing on the experimental evidence from multiple prior results. The model is well-supported by the data, though some mechanistic details (e.g., direct transcriptional regulation by JNK) could be strengthened with additional experiments.

results.result: Precocious differentiation in starved larvae may result from starvation-induced fat mobilization and increased FAO.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is speculative, as indicated by the language ('might be an outcome'). While the hypothesis is reasonable given the study's findings, no direct experimental evidence is provided to test this mechanism in starvation. This represents a testable prediction rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: JNK signaling has been previously associated with histone acetylation through Fos-Chm interactions. This study shows that JNK and Chm knockdown both block differentiation and alter H3K9/H4 acetylation, and that high ROS alone is insufficient for differentiation without functional FAO.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 integrate prior knowledge (C103-C104) with current findings (C105-C107). The experimental data showing JNK and Chm effects on differentiation and acetylation are well-supported. The conclusion that ROS is insufficient without FAO (C107) is a key insight from the elevated ROS in whd1 mutants.

results.result: Upon FAO disruption, progenitors adopt glycolysis to maintain proliferation but cannot differentiate. Glycolysis inhibition rescues proliferation defects but not differentiation, indicating that the acetyl moiety from FAO, rather than ATP production, is critical for differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 synthesize the glycolysis experiments to make a key mechanistic point: FAO's role in differentiation is through acetyl-CoA provision for acetylation, not energy production. The dissociation between proliferation and differentiation upon glycolysis inhibition (C109) is the critical evidence. This is a well-supported conclusion.

results.result: Acetyl-CoA from FAO is essential for histone acetylation and differentiation. Acetate supplementation bypasses FAO by directly providing acetyl-CoA, and AcCoAS knockdown blocks differentiation. This mechanism is conserved across model systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 synthesize the acetate rescue and AcCoAS experiments to establish the acetyl-CoA mechanism. The citations supporting acetate supplementation across organisms (C117) strengthen the significance. The biochemical explanation (C114) is well-established. The AcCoAS data (C115) provides genetic support.

results.result: FAO has been implicated in HSC maintenance through the PML-PPARδ pathway, where FAO loss causes symmetric divisions leading to stem cell exhaustion. FAO is also important in neural, muscle, and intestinal stem cells, as well as endothelial precursors.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C123 provide literature context comparing the current findings to prior work in mammalian systems. All claims are supported by citations. This discussion contextualizes the findings but notes that the role in progenitor differentiation (versus stem cell maintenance) may be distinct. This is appropriate contextualization of the work.

results.result: Drosophila blood cells are functionally similar to mammalian myeloid cells, and molecular mechanisms regulating Drosophila hematopoiesis are conserved in vertebrates, suggesting the findings may be relevant to mammalian myeloid progenitor differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 argue for the translational relevance of the findings. The citations support the functional and molecular conservation between Drosophila and mammalian hematopoiesis. This is a reasonable argument for the broader significance of the work, though direct testing in mammalian systems would be needed to confirm.
